Change it a little bit, add a few more examples so it will be a little bit more interesting. Then we will talk about marketing funnel. What is a marketing funnel? How do you build it? Then we will go into the most important concept that I told you last week. That if I want you to remember anything from this course, two years from now, three years from now, you work with another company, and you have a bunch of things. You start an engineer and they have this unbelievable disruptive technology that is gonna change the world. First question you ask them is, "Who are your customers? Let's start working on getting to our customers." Branding first. This is critical. I'll give you many examples about it. If there's anything I want you to remember is branding first. Second, we'll talk about what are the benefits of it. There are more benefits than just branding first, and questions. So I feel like I'm talking, talking, talking, and I don't know if everything I say is clear. If you have questions, I put my email address in here. If you want me — next week is our last session. All right. So what we talked last week is that innovation is evolution, which means usually it moves step by step. If somebody's making a huge leap forward, chances are nobody understands anymore. So usually when you see things, they advance step by step. And then there is the concept of enablers. Enablers is if there is something that allows the next step to happen. We talked about it, that the iPhone, for example, is a huge enabler. It had GPS in it, so suddenly you can do Tango, you can do Waze, you can do Uber, you can do Get. It's an enabler. Without iPhone or Android with the GPS in it, that won't happen, okay? So enablers bring a tremendous amount of innovation because you can use something that is already available in many, many ways.

Innovation happens concurrently, which means once the enablers are in place, you will find many companies or many people making the next step. It happens in science, for sure happens in business, happens in life. Now, I'm making here a difference between innovation and product innovation. Innovation is usually more in science, in engineering. Product innovation is when you take the enablers and you try to build something that you wanna sell to the market. Not just you wanna write an article, you wanna write a book, but you wanna sell. So product innovation has the whole level of you have to find customers, you have to convince them to buy what you were doing, and convince them to pay money. It's very, very important.

With product innovation, don't be the first. Regardless of what everybody else tells you, don't be the first. Why? If you are the first, there's a good chance you are not going to understand exactly what the market is. The first few usually come in, try something, fail, or kind of succeed. So you look at what they're doing, and you understand why they failed. And then after two, three rounds, you have a much better chance of succeeding with product innovation. And when do you succeed in product innovation? When your product reaches acceptable levels of price, performance, and ease of use. So when a product becomes stable enough, good enough for people to use, then suddenly it takes over the market. Everybody says, "Wow, it's suddenly..." It's not sudden. It's a lot of little steps until it gets to that level.

In general — iPhone, for example, right? It's kind of a general product. So it's pretty much a handheld computer. A handheld computer is a category that existed for more than twenty years before the iPhone. There were many, many versions of it. There were many, many companies in the market, including Apple with the Newton, you know, history. So it took a lot of time and many, many iterations around what features you need in there, the screen, the memory, till it reached that point.

So product innovation is not in the new technology. It's how you use the technology. That's what distinction I'm making between technology innovation, scientific innovation, and product innovation. Most product innovations are just where you wanna use it, how you wanna use it, to what purpose you wanna use it. Taxi service, we talked about it. Uber, Lyft, Get, and so forth, really came about with the iPhone, it came about with the GPS. Hotels, travel, Expedia, bookings.com, Kayak, Tripadvisor. There's nothing smart about it. But there is internet, there are databases, there are search engines, it suddenly becomes feasible. So the impact on industry — did anybody here ever use a travel agent? No. You go on the web and you book the tickets. That wasn't the case 20 years ago, and it has nothing to do with technology. That's the point I'm trying to make with you. Movie theaters, right? We still go to movie theater, not to see the movies, but more as an experience, right? You go out with friends. But to see the movies on Netflix. There was a postal service once. You can still remember. The interesting thing is the icon, right? For email. Looks like an envelope. Your kids will not understand what this icon says. Same way that the icon for a phone, you know — did anybody see anything like that? Doesn't exist anymore. Dating — well, there you can tell me, you know me. You are more expert than me. Every domain in our life is gonna be impacted by that.

So with many separation, I've brought you the book The Innovator's Dilemma. Next week, we might talk about his additional book, which is The Innovator's Solution. I haven't read it yet, so we'll see. It's a very interesting book. But sustaining innovation — what is sustaining innovation? Sustaining innovation is when there's a company that is entrenched in the market, they're a big player in the market, and they wanna innovate all the time. Why they want to innovate all the time? Because they wanna capture more and more customers, and actually, they wanna move up the price level. And so they sell something for $10, then they sell something for $15, even though it costs the same as the other one. So the innovation is usually about going up the price level. Some examples — iPhone, flat TV, right? There used to be TVs, now they have flat TVs. What is the flat TV innovation? Bigger and bigger and bigger screens. Putting an application into the TV. Nothing earth-shattering, but that's what sustaining innovation is. I also brought something non-technical. Herbal tea, one percent milk, soy milk, and a car reverse camera. Why do I bring you that? Because here what happened, you started putting screens so you can connect the iPhone. Now you have a screen, it makes sense to put a camera, and now you can do the reverse with the camera looking backwards. You can see again, the sustaining innovation is incremental innovation. One thing immediately leads to the next thing, it immediately leads to the next thing, and so on and so on. Typically, sustaining innovation is about profits.

And so what is disruptive innovation? So disruptive innovation, there are two branches. One is low-end disruption. What is low-end disruption? Essentially, it's a business model that disrupts the existing model. Give you a story. I was living in the US, and one day a guy called me, "You know, I'm using this product, I don't remember the name of it, to shave. It's basically a razor, and you pay a dollar and they send you every month, 30 razors." I said, "What's unique about it?" He said, "Nothing, except that it's very convenient. I get it every month, and I don't have to pay these enormous prices of Gillette." Turns out this company became so successful selling a product from 150 years ago that at the end, Gillette bought it for a billion dollars. Which shows you what is the innovation in here. Nothing about the razor or anything. It's just about the business model. Netflix did the same, and many other companies. You can see the disruption is not something crazy. It's just the way they do business.

And there is the market disruption. When companies develop a product, nobody wants it. And then they kind of use the product for other purposes, and it creates a whole different market. The example that the book brings is the disk drive, where the sizes of the disk become smaller and smaller, enabled the disk drives to be implemented into different pieces of equipment, like cameras and like this hard drive. This is the disruptive market as well.

The main point in here, which I think is important to think about, usually these new innovations are inferior to what exists. So if you compare this Gillette razor, it was a really dumb razor compared to old-fashioned razors. But you got it in the mail every month. It was cheap. It was inferior. It wasn't all of the big features that you want, but they disrupted the market. And once they started selling more and more, they had enough resources to keep improving and improving and improving until they became a real threat.

So think about all of this. So the five principles that we discussed. Number one, companies depend on existing customers. So that's what we said before, okay? The existing players, the big players really wanna go up the scale. They wanna sell more and more to their existing customers. And the whole DNA of the company becomes focused on serving their existing customers. If you recall, I talked to you about my personal experience at ZoomInfo, where we tried to introduce a low-end market. Didn't work. Why? Because the DNA of the company resisted.

Number two is okay, but look at these big markets and the PC, these kind of things. How come companies miss it? Well, they missed it because at the beginning, these are small markets. Small markets don't interest big companies. Why? Because they have the DNA that is heavy, and they can't deal with small markets. It's just not effective, not profitable for them to do. And also, it's hard for them to evaluate the real size of the potential market. Most potential markets don't turn out to be big. That's another lesson that many founders find. They come up with this great idea — anybody should see this is gonna buy. The reality of it is most of these products, most of these innovations go away.

Give you an example. The pharmaceutical companies used to have huge research organizations to come up with new drugs. And they were working on many ideas. Most of these ideas failed, and it became expensive for them to do it. In the last ten years, the pharmaceutical companies took a very, very different approach. They let startups develop and innovate on drugs or on treatments. If these treatments get to successful Phase II clinical trials, they acquire them, but they usually acquire them in a very bizarre way. They pay the cost of the trials. If the trials succeed, then they have an option to buy the company. If the trials fail, they just don't continue to invest in the trials. So they kind of spread their bets, and they don't do the innovation themselves. It happens a lot. As I said about Google and Android, when they realized they need an iPhone-compatible product, they bought the company. That's because markets are very hard to predict. And so what they want is to just buy proved or proven markets and not take the risk.

The organization capabilities also define its limitations and disabilities. We talked about it as well, that there is a DNA to a company, and once there is a big change, it's very hard for the company to change what they do. We discussed Kodak. That was actually a chemical manufacturing company. When you do digital photography, you don't need it. We talked about Blockbuster, that they had all of these stores with lots of inventory. You don't need it.

But look at it differently. Let's compare Netflix to Blockbuster. So Netflix had a very interesting advantage. If you send — I mean, I'm talking about the original Netflix, sending you CDs or videos every month. You just go on the web, you choose what you want, like a library, and they send it to you by mail. What that allows you to do is to keep far more titles in your inventory than if you're a physical store. A physical store, you wanna have ten copies of all the hot movies, but how many other movies can you keep on the shelf in every store? You can't. So you have maybe thousand, two thousand titles. If you have one central location, you can have a hundred thousand titles. Why? Because if anybody wants it, you ship it. If the second person wants it, they will buy this one, you know, because it's like a library. So Netflix was already in the position that they can satisfy the needs of people who wanted to have, let's call it, rare or not popular movies, where Blockbuster was never there. So the audience was much more focused.

And the performance — we talked about it at the beginning many, many times in the innovation. The initial performance doesn't fit what the main market needs. But they penetrate, and then they keep improving. Give you an example. Let's say you wanna develop a new food, and you focus this new food on people with some limitations. Lactose intolerant, something else. Okay? You develop it for that, and the taste is, ah, so-so. But people who have these limitations wanna buy something new that they're really wanting. And if it becomes a successful test, now you have the resources and the market to start improving your product, and gradually you can move into the main market. So it happens a lot when you go after a very niche need, and it's big enough to allow you to build the infrastructure and improve, you can move on to a bigger market.

Okay, branding first. The idea here is you have to start selling basically or creating a brand way before you start your product. Why? Because paying customers are hard to get. How many of you pay the bills in the bank? If you have to pay the bills, you think twice before you spend. So paying customers are hard to get. Once you ask people to put their hand in their pocket, it's not easy. The first thing you need to focus on is your prospects and customers, and the question means, who are your customers? How do you get their attention? And how do you market? How do they buy from you?

Okay, let's start with the old-fashioned way. So we didn't invent branding and marketing or whatever. So I wanna show you how companies solved it in the prehistoric era before the Internet. There was life before, check. So how did they do it? Let's take a very simple, broad example. Tambo. What did they do? They went to hardware stores, and they said, "I'm gonna give you a sign for free, and I even put your name on it, and you agree to put it on your store." Now they started having their name all over. Right? You see it everywhere. Then what happened? Their name became the noun, right? So now it's Tamboya. You see this guy? There are two signs, Tambor and Nerlat, okay, the competitors, right? So now Nerlat is at a disadvantage because you have their name everywhere. So you can see the power of branding first. You create the brand, people know about you. Even though the store sells a million other things, but your name is on this store.

So the idea here is instead of building your company around the product idea, you want to build it around branding and marketing instead. And what I want to do now is take you through several examples. Many of them are companies that I built or am building right now, so we can talk from first-person experience, what we do. And you will see the impact of what happens when you do marketing first.

So what is a brand first? I say all the time, branding, marketing, kind of interchangeably, but it's not the same. A brand has very limited requirements. You don't want people to know exactly your product features and how much it costs, different ways, but it's not the point. A brand is like a Tamboya. Oh, that's a store. I know where it is. I know that they sell paint, and that's about it. All right. But they're a good company because I see their name everywhere. So a brand is a name you want your customer to trust. Note, you want them to have a positive feeling. Feeling is not logic. It's not facts. Okay? We don't get married because of logic and facts. We get married because of feelings. So you want your customers to get married with you, not to buy your logic. We talked about Apple and how people stand in line at midnight to get the first iPhone model. And you don't need to be specific about what your product does. Remember I talked about the Kardashians and asked you what do they do? We don't know, but if they offer another clothing or whatever, we're gonna look at it.

Building a brand takes time. It's just that. It takes a lot of exposures. People — from one-time exposure, people will forget. Research shows you need at least six exposures before you start paying attention. Six. Which is why you see advertising repeating itself often. So to build a brand, you want people to be exposed to your brand many, many times.

So we talked about long tail. I'm going to spend a lot of time on examples of long tail. So SEO means search engine, and Google is your best friend. What do I mean by best friend? The purpose of Google is to have you come back to Google. So Google is very keen on measuring all the time how happy people are with their service. What is their service? Did I give you what you needed in the first spot? That's what they measure. So if you ask "What's the exchange rate of the dollar?" they won't give you a site. They will just tell you it's three sixty-eight. They give you an answer. And you ask, "When is the train to Tel Aviv?" And they give you an answer. They spend a good amount of time to make sure that you get the answers you want. What does that mean for companies? That means if they think that your page is gonna give the answer that the user wants, they will show your name or your page, and then they measure it. If people click on it or don't click on it — remember, they also give you two or three lines of content. If nobody clicks on it, you're out. If somebody clicks on it, then they measure how long they stay there. So if somebody clicks and a second later they see them back clicking on the next answer in Google — and actually between two and eight, they follow you through Chrome. You don't know that, but the whole idea of having Chrome browser is because they control the Chrome browser, so they see everything you do. Every movement of your mouse, they see that. So they look at what people do. If people stay on your page, they will raise you in their ranking. The more people click on it, the more people stay on the site, the higher the ranking you're gonna get. Why? Because Google want happy customers.

When we talked about the long tail, what is a long tail? So there are two kinds of keywords. What they call head keywords, which is common keywords, right? I want flights. I want car insurance, whatever it is. So those, everybody competes in them. Everybody. Chances are that the established companies that already proved to Google that people come to them, stay with them — they won't let an upstart take it. So what do you do? You spend money on advertising. We don't like spending money. Not good idea. So what do you do? You do long tail. Long tail means instead of having a word, you try to use a phrase, and the longer the phrase, the better. So more specific items like eighteen inch silver necklace with a pendant. It has two issues. Issue number one is you get a very low search volume. How many people search for that? Not twenty people or whatever. So the number of variations is huge. Therefore, you need to create a very large number of pages, and that's expensive. Secondly, you want your prospects or your customers to come to these pages. So the words that you are doing have to relate to the brand you wanna create. If I sell diapers and I talk about cars, yeah, maybe I'll get traffic, but it does nothing for me. So you have to find an area where you can build a long tail — and I'll talk about it at length in a moment — that your prospects are likely to be searching. That is why this strategy is tremendously effective and very, very hard. You need a lot of keywords, that your prospects are looking for them, that you have an easy way of creating these tens of thousands of pages, and that in the aggregate you get enough traffic.

So the way you do it is with a database, and I'll show you here a few examples of how you create these databases. The beauty of a database is that essentially every line in a database — think about a database as an Excel spreadsheet. Every line is an entity, a person, a country, a company, a picture, a movie, you name it, okay? And the columns are some attributes. We take a movie, then the first column will be, of course, the name of the movie, the main actors, the producer, and so on. You know, won the Oscar, didn't win the Oscar, whatever it was. So it's very easy to take a database. Each line will become a page in your website, and the content, you organize it on the page in a way that is very useful and easy for people to interact. That's how you do it.

So how you choose this set — as I said, it has to appeal to your prospects or customers. It has to be something that they look for when they do their job. So how do you do that? Remember what I said, branding first. That means you don't have the product. So what Oxita did, as I told you, is the DevOps engineer gets the market for Elasticsearch platform, which is a database. Very obscure stuff. So I asked the founder, what do DevOps engineers do when they have a problem? And after a lot of thinking, we found that they have error logs. So here's an error: "Could not lock, index writer is locked." Another one is "Delaying the location for blah blah blah." Tons of garbage. This is definitely long tail because nobody's gonna compete with you on these phrases. Nobody. And the people who search for these error logs, there's only one kind of people who do — DevOps engineers of Elasticsearch. Right? So it fulfills all what you need, except for one thing. What do you write on the page? Okay, so you have an error log. You know that the right people are looking for it, but what do you write on the page? So we cheated. We basically created kind of a standard page that says, "Oh, this is an error in Elastic," something like that, stupid like that. We made it a little bit smarter than that, but it wasn't tremendously useful. However, because we were the only people in the world that built a page for that error log, Google did present us. So we got a sample of the interest, and we found that about forty, fifty pages represented eighty percent of the traffic. That means that out of the eight hundred or nine hundred error logs, we only needed to pay attention to about fifty. And then we just did research, we figured out what the error log means, and we wrote really good content about it. And writing the good content became the foundation of all of our strategy of content. So you start seeing how this methodology starts to change what the company is.

You start with branding, and when you work on the branding, you gradually evolve your business strategy. And I'll give you many, many examples of how that happened. So this idea of branding first is not just "it's good to have customers." It has tremendous impact on what you do later on. So this is it. I show you that we put an error log, and here's what Google returned. That's real return. And we're the number one answer on Google. And we are ahead of Elastic itself and Stack Overflow, which is the most known website for developers.

Okay. So here are the traffic results for a quarter. As you can see, the company started in twenty nineteen, so this is about a year into it. We did a little bit over ten thousand visitors a month. And at the end of twenty twenty-two, which is two years later, we did about a hundred thousand visitors a month. And you can see the growth. Where is the growth coming from? Very interesting. The growth is coming from Google pushing our results higher and higher on the page. Because honestly, I don't think that people were searching for more error logs because of us. I think that the number of searches was always about the same. But Google started to trust our content, and therefore, if there was an answer for Oxita, they moved it up in their answers. The higher you are in the list, the higher the chance people click on it. So what you're seeing here is why it takes so long to build a brand. Google is very, very slow because they don't want their customers to lose something. So it takes time for Google to develop trust and confidence in your responses.

But let's talk about what does it mean to get a brand, and where does it take us? So a marketing funnel — everybody in marketing knows this, that's probably the second class in marketing that you will have. What is a funnel? A funnel starts with the space between the title and the description, which means all the people in the world who know nothing about us. And our first target is to get them to be aware of us, something about us. This is the first step when you sell. You want people to be aware of you. If I take an example, you go to a party, I assume most of you get dressed nicely. Put on your best face because you want the other people to pay attention. So that's called awareness. There's a party with 50 people. Think about a party with five billion people sitting on the web, okay? You want them to be aware of you. So that's the first thing. Branding first deals with awareness. You want people to be aware. But then that's not enough, because being aware of you — you want them to invite you for a dance, right? So there should be some engagement before they start considering maybe I wanna invite you also to dinner. So dress nicely, a buddy invites you to dance, then dinner, and then everything else.

So you need also to get engagement. So in the process of building your marketing strategy, you say, "Okay, I got them to my webpage," but we will later on see other mechanisms of getting the awareness. How do I move them down the marketing funnel all the way to conversion? Conversion means buying. You see the line between marketing and sales, okay? I want them to move to the green. So I need to do something or have them do something to move from awareness to engagement, to consideration, to buying.

So let's see what we did. So with Optima, what we did is the following. They have a problem, right? They got an error they want to show off, and we wanted to develop something that will be easy to use, free, and useful. So we came up with the idea of a checkup. What is a checkup? This is it. Welcome to OptiMine checkup. Here's the file I want you to give me, and I'll do like a blood test. If you allow me to prick your finger and take some blood, I'll tell you what's going on. So they give us this file, we analyze it, and we actually did a pretty good job of giving them pretty insightful information about their ElasticSearch clusters. Along the way, if you wanted to see your results, you had to register. So we had twelve thousand users who registered, and that became our main source of leads, because now we have your name and we have your contact information. Okay, so you see how you take awareness and you start moving it down the funnel. So you wanna move them to engagement. Engagement means they have to do something and hopefully leave a trail of how to get back. So here are the numbers. We started with 88 in Q3 of 2020, and we ended up with 13,000 a few years later. It takes time to build it as well, and that was the main source of our business.

Any questions on OptiMine and what I said until now? All right. So this is another — as I told you, I'm gonna talk about companies I'm heavily involved in, so I know all the dirty secrets. GiveChop. Has anybody here ever encountered GiveChop? Okay, what do they do? They basically — it's a platform to sell tickets. Small company, about 30 employees in Jerusalem. The web platform for building event pages. So if you are a speaker, an artist, a lecturer, whatever, you wanna have 50 people in a room, you want them to buy tickets, you need to put up a page, and you need to allow people to click buy a ticket, put their credit card, and get a ticket. That's what they do. Basically, a platform to allow anybody to build an event page and sell tickets. The entire process is digital. They send the ticket back to you on your phone with an SMS or WhatsApp, and they handle the credit card processing, and they take a five percent commission, and that's how they make money, and they were profitable from inception. They never took any investment from anybody, and they generate cash every month. So they are profitable, generating cash flow. They even survived the COVID lockdowns. As you might guess, there were no events happening for a year. And what they did is they looked at it and they figured out, actually, what we have is a platform to collect money from people. So instead of selling events, you can sell charity. They took a commission from the donations? Yes. Smaller, much smaller, like two percent. And they were profitable even then, and also they got back money from the government.

Then they invented the name GiveChop. And they grow nicely, 20% year over year, every year thereafter. Why did they talk to us? They said, "We're stuck in Sharon." I said, "What does that mean?" And they said, "Well, we feel like we go word of mouth, you know, in our own little circle, but we want to become known in the entire country — in Israel — and then we wanna move international." And we have no idea how to do that. So that's where they were, and since you guys now, after one and a half lectures about branding first, I'm sure you can tell me what should we do?

Okay, I'll save you the pain. Long tail style. So what we wanted to do is have a database of every event, current and past, of every singer, artist, actor, stand-up comedian, anybody who does anything in Israel, and sell tickets. So there are about 25 or 30 ticket offices, basically websites where you can buy tickets in Israel, and obviously they publish information, right? Because they want everybody to be able to buy a ticket. So we built a little bot, and the bot every morning goes and visits all of these 25 or 30 online websites and scrapes all the information about new events and any changes to existing events. So every day we get a full list of all the events that are gonna happen in Israel, every single day. And for each one, we extract the information from there. So it's not very difficult. We wanna know the name of the concert, the type of the event — was it jazz, rock, lecture, stand-up, classical music, whatever it is. Why? Because then we want to allow people to search by whatever they want. The name of the artist or artists, the date and the time of the event, the venue, where it's gonna happen, the location, the city, the price range. Whatever we can find on this, we collect. Now what do we have? A database. Every line is an event, and every column is the data. Not complicated.

And we build a summary page. Now what we do with this is we are a little bit more creative. So we take this information, and we actually organize it in various ways. For example, we can collect all the information about a singer and say, "Here's what this singer does and did. Here are all the events that this singer had. Here's his bio. Here are his pictures. Here are the lyrics. Here's his Facebook page. Here is his Spotify link, YouTube." You name it. There aren't that many people. There are about 5,000 artists in Israel, so we were able to gradually build a full page per artist. Tremendously valuable. If you like classical music, I can give you all the shows. If you like stand-up comedy, whatever it is, we can do that. The venue, you wanna know what's in HaHakatut this month, the city — and so on.

So this is Hanan Ben Ari. That's the page, and it has more information. That's his Wikipedia page and all the other information. And you see the branding. They started putting a brand. That's on the top here, and it says "Tikshat Live," "Pokata Hachutz." Small, tiny company they are, Pokata Hachutz. And when you run a Google search for Hanan Ben Ari, here's what you get. Tikshat is the first. Then Memabim, and then Kukot Tel Aviv, which is where you buy tickets for this show. Not bad.

Now the question is, all right, but they sell tickets, and we do this Big Track Live. What is the audience we're trying to attract, and why? Remember, for us to make money, for Ticket to make money, they need to actually talk to the producer, the manager, or the artist who sell the tickets. The people who buy the ticket don't pay us anything. And so if we don't have the right to sell the tickets, why are we doing it? Now when you have visitors to the website, and you have a business case that you can talk with the producer — very good. Any other ideas? What else can we do with this?

So we have three different audiences actually. The people who wanna buy tickets for the show. The artists, the managers, the producers who want to sell tickets via our platform. And also the venues and the cities. So what do we wanna accomplish? Let's start. People who wanna go to a show. So what we did is we built a process to collect contact information of fans and followers of the artist. How does it work? When you wanna buy a ticket, you click on buy a ticket. We have this pop-up. And the pop-up says, "Be the first to get any information on this artist." So now you say, "Oh, sure. Why not? I'll get information." So you put in your email address or your phone number or whatever it is. We start collecting information about fans and followers of the artist. This is our information. They're visiting our site. They have the relationship with us, not with the artist, not with the producer, not with the manager. It's an asset. Using this growing list, we offer the artist tools to interact with their fans. Remember, because Google gives us first, there's a good chance they will go through our website, click on buy a ticket, they go to the original place they sell the ticket. But along the way, we tell them, "Why don't you leave your information in this?" So we start building assets that were not in the original business model to begin.

So I'm starting to take you through how branding first allows you to build businesses you didn't think about. Okay? So with that, what you can do is you tell the artist, "Listen, you can build — potentially, you can sell a lot of tickets day one by creating this elite group of followers who will get access to the tickets a day before everybody else, so they can pick any seat they want because they're the first." Why is it important for the artist? Because nobody wants an empty hall. So they wanna make sure in the beginning that they kind of fill up thirty, forty percent of the place before they even go out there. Same goes for the end. So it's the last day, and fifty percent of the seats are empty. So you're in a rush to get to people who are likely to come to your show. We can build this.

What about intellectual property — do we need special permission to do all this? You ask a really good question. We get, not a lot, but about one email a month from producers and managers who say, "You have no right to do what you do." The answer is, yes, we do. These are facts. Nobody owns facts. The fact that an artist has a concert in a hall on Tuesday is a fact. It's nothing unique. We don't sell the tickets — we transfer them to the original site. So we're just a link along the way. And what we said, there are very clear disclaimers. We don't sell the tickets. We take you back to the original site. We don't wanna get in trouble. So you're basically just stating something that is on the internet already. Yes. When you get to intellectual property, that's the first thing you want to understand — what people have intellectual property on and what they don't. Nobody has intellectual property on facts.

So these are the offerings for the artists, right? Three basic offerings. You can own your page and make it your home page. Now, like anything else, there's a long tail. There may be twenty top artists. And then there's a long tail of artists and stand-up comedians or whatever that don't fill up Tel Aviv, but they're doing okay. They can't really afford to have a manager. They build their own website, and their Facebook page looks utterly junk. So here we give them a nice page that we maintain, that includes all of their shows, current and past. So we put them in a much higher level, and we give them tools to add pictures, add information, do all of that stuff. And we give them then access to the list of their fans and followers, so they can communicate with them — but that's the paid option.

So you start to see how we add value to everybody, and at the same time, we build additional revenue sources that were not in the original plan at all. And in the end, obviously, we would like them to move over to us, so we can sell all of that. That's why we wanted to also collect information about cities because some cities, Jerusalem for sure, want to have on their website all the shows happening in Jerusalem in the next week or month. So they have six people that look at newspapers and all that and do it manually, and we very graciously say, "Maybe you can just license the data from us. We can even build it for you, and everything is always updated."

What are the benefits of doing this? So before you spend a huge amount of money and development on building your product, there are benefits to doing what I just described. First thing is companies have to be profitable. Profitable — my definition here is cash generated. What you want is at the end of every month, your bank account has money in it. Because as a company, we need blood in order to live, right? The day our blood goes away, we die. Money is the blood of the company. No money, the company is out. So you want to get to money as fast as possible. For that, you need customers, and you need sales. Okay? So you need to build all of that stuff as early as possible. I showed you why it takes time to do it. And the customers will not come unless they know about you — the awareness. Okay? And unless they have positive feelings towards you.

And very important thing, there's no way to always address the whole market. Right? So to do effective branding, you need what's called a beachhead. Anybody here knows what a beachhead is? The World War II, D-Day, June fifth, nineteen forty-four, the invasion of the Allies. When Nazi Germany controlled from Norway in the north all the way down to France in the south, five thousand kilometers long, fortified wall. The beachhead of Normandy was only eighty kilometers. So the entire US, UK, and other Allies armies were going on a stretch of eighty kilometers out of five thousand. So they put all of their efforts in a very, very small area. Why? Because in that small area, they can overwhelm the enemy. If they try to send a soldier per kilometer, he will get killed. So a beachhead means you wanna focus all your attention on a very, very small market segment so that you become bigger than life. Remember, you need a brand. So you can try to spread your efforts over a very large market — nobody hears about you. Or you narrow it, and suddenly for this narrow group, you're bigger than life.

You all feel it when you go on the web. You're looking at, I don't know, fertilizer for your garden, and everywhere you go, every page you go, you see advertising for that stupid fertilizer, right? That's the most common advertising practice. Why? Because they want to overwhelm you. So they put a cookie, and now they're bigger than life. You see them all the time. But that's the same idea. You want to be bigger than life for a very specific thing, for a very specific person. What you wanna hear is — the idea of branding first is you kind of spread the word, and you wanna see who is going to raise their hand.

So you said, "Okay, I wanna sell tickets for all of these five thousand artists." Who is going to do that? I don't know. But I can tell you that in the coming weeks or months, some of them will call us and say, "Hey, you know, this is really cool. How do I do X?" And we start looking at who is calling us, who is talking to us, and that becomes our beachhead because usually there's a reason why a certain group of people should call us. Maybe it's all the people who just give lectures. Maybe it's the people who do stand-up comedy. I don't know who it's gonna be, but there's gonna be a group of people who will raise their hand. And now we say, "Okay, is it ten of you? There are another hundred? Let's go after the hundred because we have a story to tell them." The interesting thing about what I said, in a way, you solve two problems at once. One is you kind of figure out what is your beachhead — who are the people that really get impacted, they have good feelings, they want what you're doing, they raise their hand. Number two is they did it, so you have now an effective way of reaching out to them. So usually what you do in marketing is you say, "Okay, I want to get to these kind of people. Now I need to start thinking, where do I advertise? How much money I spend?" In this case, the way you know who they are is the way they communicate with you. So you already created the engagement basis, okay? Already as part of the branding. And that's tremendously powerful because you save huge amount of time and money.

And what also happens is what I said several times in here, that this process usually evolves and changes what you think about the product you want to sell. New opportunities show up, new ideas come up, your business model changes. A lot of things happen along the way. And all of that time, you spend very little money.

Okay, so I want to talk about another company in here. So another company that we have is called IntelliChain, and they are demand planning software. At the low end of the market. What is demand planning? Every company that sells something — Coca-Cola, whatever it is — have a lot of products that they need to produce. They wanna know how many yogurts they have to produce, how many cottage cheese they have to produce every day, every week, every month. And that's based on their anticipation or planning for the demand. All right? So if I try to sell my salt on Sukkot, probably the demand will be zero. If I do it two weeks before Passover, it's gonna be probably selling out very well. So I need to understand what I'm doing. So there is software that they developed that allows you to put in historical demand and do predictions based on all kinds of things. That's what they do. It's a piece of S&OP — Sales and Operations Process. The idea is you want all the groups in the company to talk to one another about what they do. So if sales say, "I'm going to do a promotion, and I wanna have five thousand more yogurts with egg flavor," then somebody has to produce the five thousand egg flavor yogurt. So you need to have coordination in the company. It's a small company, maybe ten, twenty employees. Joined us in April twenty twenty-six.

The product is a sophisticated module aimed at the low end of the market. And what we realized fairly quickly is that it's a hard sell. Long sales cycle, and customers wanted to see it working — what's called a proof of concept. That means we needed to spend a few days working with the customer, taking all of their historical data, churning it, running, preparing a presentation. Tremendous amount of work, and no sales. So what we did in the proof of concept, we did an analysis of the inventory because a lot of companies have a few hundred items they produce themselves. Not all of them are best sellers. The question is, do they have the right inventory? Not too much for products that don't sell well, and not too little for products that sell well and they run out. So they want to balance their inventory, and it turns out that's not an easy task, and that's what usually what we show. And when they showed it to the customer, usually the proof of concept, the customer said, "Wow, that's really interesting," and they didn't buy it.

So listen again — "Wow, so interesting," and they didn't buy it. If you guys are gonna be entrepreneurs, expect people to hand you nice words. "It's so interesting, you know." "Yeah, really, that's cool. Wow." "Uh, it's ten thousand dollars." "Oh yeah, uh, let me check." Nothing happens, right?

So we wanted to do the usual long tail market. Except for one big problem — nothing we did seemed to work. So we took a very different marketing approach. What happened is that the founder was many years at Ernst & Young, which is a big consulting firm. He specialized in S&OP practice, worked with dozens of customers, trained them, and had a lot of training experience and training material. So instead of selling a product that most customers didn't really understand, we started selling training courses. Why is selling training courses easy? Because everybody knows what a training course is. It's right here. You sit in the class. There's a person whose job is to entertain you. You get a nice card at the end. Everybody knows what it means. S&OP sounds really fancy. Now I'll come back after two days and tell everybody how smart I am.

And here's what started to happen. So people register, right? We do it on the web. They register, and then we call them and we say, "By the way, we really want you to benefit from this training. For that, we really want to understand what your needs are so that we can tailor the course to your needs. So can we spend a few minutes on the phone so you will tell me what your needs are?" Usually, this is called a sales call. Nobody likes sales calls. But in this case, it's not a sale. You tell me what you want me to talk about in the training course you already registered and you're gonna pay for. So we get a lot of potential customers on the phone, and we understand what they are doing. So you start seeing the marketing funnel happening. And this is a paid sales call because they pay us for the training. We're now working on the first international training course. It's gonna launch in early March, and it's gonna cost two thousand dollars per person. So if we get fifty people, that's a hundred thousand dollars. There are ten people on the team, so they're gonna be profitable just on this.

But I'm trying to show you here how you start thinking about branding and the company starts to evolve. And this is not just marketing. This is about the strategy of the company. Who am I talking to? What am I saying to them? And suddenly things change as you do it. So what we do in the course is we start telling them about inventory balancing, all the stuff I was telling you. And we show them how you do that using the product of IntelliChain. Customer says, "Oh, wow, that's really cool. I wonder what it would do in my company." So we sell them strategic consulting. Wonderful name. Strategic — everybody likes strategic. Everybody knows what it is. I pay by the hour, by the project, whatever it is — ten thousand dollars. So we even didn't start selling the product for ten thousand dollars. We're now selling training, and then this strategic consulting. So we agree on ten thousand dollars, and I sit with the guy, the president, and I look at the pipeline of deals we have, and suddenly I see strategic consultant at forty thousand dollars. I said, "Roy, what's going on? We agreed at ten thousand. Why did you put forty?" "I don't know. He was so excited, and he seemed to be willing to pay more, so I said forty and he didn't blink. So I took forty." So you see how things happen.

So now we have a funnel. Remember we talked about the funnel. Awareness — selling training courses. It's easy. We advertise it. People respond to it. That's easy. They come to the course. I do a sales call before. I understand better who they are. At the course, I start explaining to them about what they're gonna learn about and the strategic consulting. And as we were doing that, you could start seeing the awareness, the engagement, the consideration happening.

But — and here comes the big but. So S&OP is a hot topic. Everybody's talking about it in these circles. But it turns out, like anything else I told you, when you have a new innovation, it takes a pretty long time to take root. So everybody's talking about it, but very few are doing it. They're willing to come to the course, they are willing to get consultation, they want to educate themselves, but they're not moving to actually buying products. So the biggest competitor, which is a big company called GEA, their product is like two hundred and fifty thousand dollars. It has three systems in use. Three. That's all. Nothing. Why? Because the market is just not ready.

Luckily, we discovered it through this process fairly early and came up with a different strategy. Now, why is it not selling? Because it is scary. Complicated, expensive, and painful to implement. We compare it to starting a diet. Simple, right? Stop eating. So we all wake up in the morning and we say, "That's it. I start my diet. I'm going to lose ten pounds." For two days, I only eat vegetables. I'm really good at it. But after a week, I really want something sweet. After a month, I forget about it. I gain back all the weight I lost. That's exactly what turned out in this. It's a concept that you need to do. It's painful because it requires a lot of stuff to happen, and companies, even when they start and pay all the money and get all the consultation, don't really sustain it.

So we came up with a different concept called agile SME. Anybody here knows what agile computing is and how you develop software with agile? So it's a term used a lot in software development. But instead of having big projects with a big beginning and very clear steps along the way, you move to "Let's do something and update it every week." Every week we have a meeting, we talk about what we're doing and we keep changing. So we said, "Wait a minute. Let me see how you can take a monolithic process that took years and cost a lot of money and convert it to something agile." So literally, about three days ago, we invented this concept. We already bought the website agilecm3.com. We got all the government documents and everything. We bought it for nine dollars each. And we're now building software that will support this process. For agile software engineering, there is a process and there is software to do that. And so what you're seeing here is, again, completely changing the direction of the company by generating revenues from every step.

So I wanted to show you, everything is long tail, but not everything should be done purely as long tail. But the concept of you have to be out in the market, build the brand, talk to customers, move them from awareness to engagement — that has to happen very, very early. And when you start thinking about it and doing it, things change, things happen.

So when you talk about product innovation, that's my advice. Because when I said at the beginning, anything you remember — that's the only thing I want you to remember. Don't get stuck on "I have this disruptive idea, this battery that flies in the air," whatever. Forget about it. Who's gonna buy it?

So we basically need to sell a product before we create the company? Yes. But we need to build something in order to sell something, no? That's correct. But here comes the hard facts of life. You will have a really hard time selling anything, built or not built. So you better encounter all the troubles of selling a product when it's still on paper. You can show it on the screen. Remember, most times nowadays you don't see the customer. You work on Zoom, you share screens. What do you have on the screen? Whatever you want to put on the screen. So it's not a product. You show wireframes, you click on a button, it moves, it does all the things you hope it does behind, but it shows what it does. Then you will be shocked to see how difficult it is to sell, even when you pretend you have it. But what you gain is: Who is interested? Why are they interested? What do they tell me? How much money are they willing to pay? You have plenty of time, trust me. Plenty of time.

Let me give you a few more ideas on how you do the branding, and then we'll wrap up. So there are some other methodologies that we have developed — how you build a brand, not just the examples I showed you. Two examples that are radically different. Basically, we have nothing — no idea — and we want to penetrate a market. You kind of define the market. Let's say it's the market of dentists or whatever. What you wanna do is position yourself as the expert in the market. Well, that's easier said than done, right? How do you position yourself as the expert in the market? So what you do is the following. You take a list of, let's say, five hundred dentists, and you send them an email with a questionnaire with three or four questions. Are you using this sophisticated new technology? Yes or no? If no, why not? If yes, why yes? Whatever it is. Doesn't really matter. Most doctors will ignore you. But ten or fifteen will respond. So now you create a presentation and you say, "Well, we did a deep market research, and we found out that this technology is not yet right," blah blah blah, which is based on real facts — fifteen people. And two weeks later, you send the next questionnaire, but this time you attach to it the results from the previous questionnaire. So now you are legit, right? You are legit. This is what we talked about this technology. Now we're checking a different technology. Now you will get thirty responses because you have proved you are serious.

After a few iterations — that's why I call it evolving — gradually, you will become the expert. Not because of yourself, but the market will start thinking about you as the expert. And they will wanna start reading what you write because you're doing some interesting research among their peers, and you get interesting results. And now when you talk about your own product, people listen, because you're the expert. So that is kind of a very generic process you can do virtually in every industry. You have to become the expert. They call it now the thought leader in the market. But you can become the thought leader very easily because it's easy to send questionnaires to people. Some of them will respond, and you will start getting traction. It is interesting because it is real. It's people responding.

Now, sometimes it even creates income opportunity. So just out of a joke, I said, "How many fishing magazines are there?" There are about forty-plus, counting all of that. Why would that generate revenues? Because a lot of people wanna reach these people and sell them fishing rods and tackle, whatever. There's always somebody else who wants to reach these people and do the work. So if you start penetrating the dentists and you have a newsletter that is read by a hundred thousand dentists, because you are the thought leader in the dentistry industry, and you talk about new technology — every two weeks, you send a newsletter — then people who wanna advertise on this will pay you. As surprising as it sounds. So what you do by going branding first, you start creating assets. They're worth money and make your life so much easier when you want to sell your new drill.

What I wanted to show you here is three companies that actually built their entire business on purpose from the beginning on a long tail strategy. Indeed — a recruiting platform. Zillow — real estate. And Yelp. All right. So the three of them actually started and continued to be based on long tail. Let's start with Indeed. So it was founded in November two thousand and four. And what they did was very similar to what ZoomInfo did. They crawled the internet and looked for job postings, whether it's on company websites or on job boards or whatever, and aggregated all of that. And they published it. Each job offer was published on a different page, and they collected a lot of data around it, tabulated it for Google, so that if Google wanted to show you ads for, I don't know, product manager in a certain industry, they showed Indeed first. They now have fifteen thousand employees. Twenty years to get there.

Zillow. They showed information about every address, and the most important thing — this is the engagement — they want you to own that listing. And to do that, you need to pay them a little bit of money. So they're basically a real estate platform. But they did it very, very smart. They just took every single address in the US, and there's a lot of information in many, many public records, so it wasn't difficult.

The one I like the most is Yelp. Founded in 2004, and since became one of the leading sources of user-generated reviews, mainly around business, small businesses like hairdressers, coffee shops, lawyers, things like that. And they started by publishing Yellow Pages information. Anybody can guess what Elio Technologies is? So when I started ZoomInfo back in 2000, you couldn't find a singlename.com. So I decided to use a Hebrew name, Evyon, but even that was taken, so I had to add the stupid I. So that was the name of the company back in 2004. And that's the address. Both are defunct. Company turned out to be ZoomInfo. We changed the name in 2004. And Yelp still shows the old Elio entry — from yesterday. So it shows you where the data came from. It came from the phone book. They found it. Nobody has intellectual property on facts. And that's a very important element I want you to think about.

תהליך פשוט ודדוקטיבי: קודם אומרים לאנשים מה אתם הולכים לומר להם, אחר כך אומרים להם את הדבר עצמו, ואז מסכמים ואומרים להם מה אמרתם. לכן אני רוצה להתחיל בסקירה קצרה של מה שלמדנו בשבוע שעבר. אשנה אותה קצת, אוסיף עוד כמה דוגמאות כדי שזה יהיה מעניין יותר, ואז נדבר על marketing funnel: מה זה משפך שיווקי, איך בונים אותו, ואיך משתמשים בו. אחר כך ניכנס למושג החשוב ביותר שאמרתי לכם בשבוע שעבר. אם יש דבר אחד שאני רוצה שתזכרו מהקורס הזה בעוד שנתיים או שלוש, כשאתם עובדים בחברה אחרת או פוגשים מהנדס שיש לו טכנולוגיה "משבשת" מדהימה שתשנה את העולם, השאלה הראשונה שלכם צריכה להיות: מי הלקוחות שלך? בואו נתחיל לעבוד על איך מגיעים ללקוחות. Branding first. זה קריטי. אתן הרבה דוגמאות לכך. אם יש דבר אחד שאני רוצה שתזכרו, זה branding first.

אחר כך נדבר גם על היתרונות של הגישה הזו. יש לה יתרונות רבים מעבר לעצם בניית המותג. ובנוסף, אני מרגיש שאני מדבר ומדבר ולא תמיד יודע אם הכול ברור. לכן שמתי כאן את כתובת המייל שלי. השבוע הבא הוא המפגש האחרון שלנו. אם יש משהו שאתם רוצים שאכסה, משהו שתרצו שאדבר עליו, שלחו לי מייל ואקח את זה בחשבון. אם יש לכם שאלות כלליות, גם כאן המייל. אני לא מבטיח לענות, אבל אתם יכולים לשלוח.

בשבוע שעבר דיברנו על כך שחדשנות היא אבולוציה. כלומר, בדרך כלל היא מתקדמת צעד אחר צעד. אם מישהו עושה קפיצה ענקית קדימה, הסיכוי הוא שאף אחד כבר לא יבין מה הוא עושה. לכן ברוב המקרים, כשמסתכלים על חדשנות, רואים התקדמות הדרגתית. דיברנו גם על המושג enablers, כלומר דברים שמאפשרים לצעד הבא לקרות. ה-iPhone, למשל, הוא enabler עצום. היה בו GPS, ולכן פתאום אפשר לעשות Pango, Waze, Uber, Get וכל הדברים האלה. בלי iPhone או Android עם GPS, זה לא היה קורה. Enablers מביאים כמות אדירה של חדשנות, כי הם נותנים משהו שכבר זמין, שאפשר להשתמש בו בהרבה מאוד דרכים.

חדשנות גם מתרחשת במקביל. כלומר, ברגע שה-enablers נמצאים במקום, תמצאו הרבה חברות והרבה אנשים שעושים את הצעד הבא. זה קורה במדע, זה קורה בעסקים, וזה קורה בחיים בכלל. עכשיו אני עושה כאן הבחנה בין innovation לבין product innovation. Innovation היא בדרך כלל במדע או בהנדסה. Product innovation היא כאשר לוקחים את ה-enablers ומנסים לבנות משהו שרוצים למכור לשוק. לא רק לכתוב מאמר, לא רק לכתוב ספר, אלא למכור. לכן ב-product innovation יש רובד נוסף לגמרי: צריך למצוא לקוחות, לשכנע אותם לקנות את מה שאתם עושים, ולשכנע אותם לשלם כסף. זה חשוב מאוד.

ב-product innovation, אל תהיו הראשונים. בלי קשר למה שאחרים אומרים לכם, אל תהיו הראשונים. למה? אם אתם הראשונים, יש סיכוי טוב שלא תבינו בדיוק מהו השוק. הראשונים בדרך כלל נכנסים, מנסים משהו, נכשלים או מצליחים חלקית. אתם יכולים להסתכל על מה שהם עושים ולהבין למה הם נכשלו. אחרי שניים-שלושה סבבים כאלה יש לכם סיכוי הרבה יותר טוב להצליח עם חדשנות מוצרית. מתי מצליחים ב-product innovation? כאשר המוצר מגיע לרמות מקובלות של מחיר, ביצועים וקלות שימוש. כאשר מוצר הופך יציב מספיק, טוב מספיק ושימושי מספיק, אז פתאום הוא משתלט על השוק. כולם אומרים: וואו, זה קרה פתאום. אבל זה לא פתאום. זה הרבה צעדים קטנים עד שמגיעים לרמה הזו.

ה-iPhone הוא דוגמה כללית לכך. הוא למעשה מחשב כף יד. קטגוריית מחשבי כף יד הייתה קיימת יותר מעשרים שנה לפני ה-iPhone. היו הרבה מאוד גרסאות, הרבה חברות, כולל Apple עם Newton, למי שמכיר את ההיסטוריה. לקח הרבה זמן והרבה איטרציות סביב השאלה אילו פיצ'רים צריכים להיות שם, מה צריך להיות המסך, כמה זיכרון צריך, עד שהמוצר הגיע לנקודה שבה הוא באמת עובד. לכן product innovation אינה הטכנולוגיה החדשה עצמה, אלא איך משתמשים בטכנולוגיה. איפה משתמשים בה, לאיזו מטרה משתמשים בה, ואיזה צורך היא פותרת. דיברנו על שירותי מוניות: Uber, Lyft, Get וכדומה. הם נוצרו בזכות ה-iPhone וה-GPS. דיברנו על מלונות ונסיעות: Expedia, Booking.com, Kayak, TripAdvisor. אין שם טכנולוגיה "חכמה" במיוחד. יש אינטרנט, יש databases, יש מנועי חיפוש, ופתאום זה נעשה אפשרי.

מישהו כאן השתמש פעם בסוכן נסיעות? לא. אתם נכנסים לאינטרנט ומזמינים כרטיסים. לפני עשרים שנה זה לא היה כך, וזה לא בגלל שהטכנולוגיה הבסיסית כל כך מתוחכמת, אלא בגלל שהשימוש בה השתנה. בתי קולנוע: אנחנו עדיין הולכים לקולנוע, אבל לרוב לא רק כדי לראות סרט, אלא כחוויה, כדי לצאת עם חברים. את הסרט עצמו אפשר לראות ב-Netflix. היה פעם שירות דואר. אתם עוד זוכרים. מעניין שסמל האימייל עדיין נראה כמו מעטפה. הילדים שלכם לא יבינו מה הסמל הזה אומר. אותו דבר לגבי סמל הטלפון: הוא נראה כמו מכשיר שאף אחד כמעט לא ראה כבר שנים. Dating, היכרויות — בזה אתם כבר המומחים יותר ממני. כל תחום בחיים שלנו יושפע מהדבר הזה.

הבאתי לכם את הספר The Innovator's Dilemma. אולי בשבוע הבא נדבר גם על הספר הנוסף של Christensen, שנקרא The Innovator's Solution. עדיין לא קראתי אותו, אז נראה. זה ספר מעניין מאוד. Sustaining innovation — מה זו חדשנות משמרת? זו כאשר חברה מבוססת בשוק, שחקן גדול, רוצה לחדש כל הזמן. למה היא רוצה לחדש? כי היא רוצה לתפוס עוד ועוד לקוחות, ובעיקר לעלות ברמת המחיר. היא מוכרת משהו בעשרה דולר, ואז מוכרת משהו בחמישה עשר דולר, אף על פי שהעלות שלה דומה. החדשנות היא בדרך כלל עלייה ברמת המחיר והרווחיות.

דוגמאות: iPhone. כל שנה עוד גרסה. מצלמה טובה יותר, מעבד טוב יותר, מסך טוב יותר. טלוויזיות שטוחות: פעם היו טלוויזיות, אחר כך מסכים שטוחים, ואז מסכים גדולים יותר ויותר, ואז מוסיפים אפליקציות ו-streamer בתוך הטלוויזיה. אין כאן רעידת אדמה, אבל זו sustaining innovation. הבאתי גם דוגמאות לא טכנולוגיות: תה צמחים, חלב 1%, חלב סויה, ומצלמת רוורס ברכב. למה מצלמת רוורס? כי ברגע שמתחילים לשים מסכים ברכב כדי לחבר iPhone או מערכות אחרות, הגיוני לשים מצלמה ולראות מה קורה מאחור. שוב רואים ש-sustaining innovation היא incremental innovation: דבר אחד מוביל לדבר הבא, שמוביל לדבר הבא, וכן הלאה. בדרך כלל sustaining innovation קשורה לרווחים.

ומהי disruptive innovation? יש לה שני ענפים. הראשון הוא low-end disruption. זו בעצם חדשנות במודל עסקי שמשבשת את המודל הקיים. אספר סיפור. כשגרתי בארצות הברית, יום אחד מישהו התקשר אליי ואמר שהוא משתמש במוצר כלשהו לגילוח. זה בעצם סכין גילוח, ואתה משלם דולר, והם שולחים לך כל חודש שלושים סכינים. שאלתי: מה מיוחד בזה? הוא אמר: שום דבר, חוץ מזה שזה נוח. אני מקבל את זה כל חודש ולא צריך לשלם את המחירים הענקיים של Gillette. החברה הזו הפכה כל כך מצליחה, כשהיא מוכרת מוצר שקיים כבר מאה וחמישים שנה, שבסופו של דבר Gillette קנתה אותה במיליארד דולר. מה החדשנות כאן? לא בסכין הגילוח. לא בטכנולוגיה. רק במודל העסקי. Netflix עשתה דבר דומה, ועוד חברות רבות. כלומר, disruption אינה תמיד רעיון מטורף. לפעמים זה פשוט איך עושים עסקים.

הענף השני הוא market disruption. כאן חברות מפתחות מוצר שאף אחד לא רוצה בשוק המרכזי, ואז משתמשים בו למטרות אחרות ונוצר שוק חדש לגמרי. הדוגמה מהספר היא disk drives: ככל שהדיסקים נעשו קטנים יותר, הם יכלו להיכנס לציוד אחר, כמו מצלמות או מכשירים קטנים. זו גם disruption של שוק. הנקודה העיקרית היא שבדרך כלל החדשנויות החדשות נחותות לעומת מה שקיים. סכין הגילוח ההיא הייתה די טיפשה בהשוואה לסכיני גילוח מתוחכמים. אבל קיבלת אותה בדואר כל חודש, והיא הייתה זולה. היא הייתה inferior, בלי כל הפיצ'רים הגדולים, אבל היא שיבשה את השוק. וברגע שהחברה התחילה למכור יותר ויותר, היו לה מספיק משאבים להמשיך לשפר את המוצר עד שהפכה לאיום אמיתי.

חמשת העקרונות שדיברנו עליהם: הראשון הוא שחברות תלויות בלקוחות קיימים. השחקנים הגדולים רוצים לעלות בסקאלה, למכור יותר ויותר ללקוחות הקיימים, וכל ה-DNA של החברה מתמקד בשירות הלקוחות הקיימים. דיברתי על הניסיון האישי שלי ב-ZoomInfo, כשניסינו להכניס מוצר לשוק הנמוך. זה לא עבד. למה? כי ה-DNA של החברה התנגד.

העיקרון השני: איך חברות גדולות מפספסות שווקים כמו PC? הן מפספסות כי בתחילת הדרך אלה שווקים קטנים. שווקים קטנים לא מעניינים חברות גדולות. יש להן DNA כבד, והן לא יכולות לטפל בשווקים קטנים באופן יעיל או רווחי. בנוסף, קשה להן להעריך את הגודל האמיתי של השוק הפוטנציאלי. רוב השווקים הפוטנציאליים באמת לא הופכים לשווקים גדולים. זו עוד תובנה שמייסדים רבים מגלים. יש להם רעיון גדול והם אומרים: כולם ירצו לקנות את זה. אבל במציאות רוב המוצרים ורוב החדשנויות פשוט נעלמים.

דוגמה: חברות פארמה. בעבר היו להן ארגוני מחקר עצומים לפיתוח תרופות חדשות. הן עבדו על הרבה רעיונות, ורוב הרעיונות נכשלו. זה הפך יקר מאוד. בעשר השנים האחרונות חברות פארמה עברו לגישה אחרת: הן נותנות לסטארטאפים לפתח תרופות או טיפולים. אם הטיפולים מגיעים בהצלחה ל-Phase II clinical trials, הן רוכשות אותם, בדרך מוזרה: הן מממנות את עלות הניסויים. אם הניסויים מצליחים, יש להן option לקנות את החברה. אם הניסויים נכשלים, הן מפסיקות להשקיע. כך הן מפזרות הימורים ולא עושות את כל החדשנות בעצמן. זה קורה הרבה. כמו שאמרתי על Google ו-Android: כשהם הבינו שהם צריכים מוצר שמתחרה ב-iPhone, הם קנו חברה. כי קשה מאוד לחזות שווקים, ולכן הם מעדיפים לקנות שוק מוכח מאשר לקחת את כל הסיכון.

גם היכולות הארגוניות מגדירות את המגבלות והנכויות של הארגון. דיברנו על כך שיש DNA לחברה. כאשר יש שינוי גדול, קשה מאוד לחברה לשנות את מה שהיא עושה. Kodak הייתה למעשה חברת ייצור כימית. כשיש צילום דיגיטלי, כבר לא צריך את היכולות הכימיות שלה. Blockbuster החזיקה חנויות עם הרבה מלאי. בעולם של streaming לא צריך את זה.

אבל אפשר להסתכל על זה אחרת: נשווה Netflix ל-Blockbuster. Netflix המקורית שלחה לכם DVD או וידאו כל חודש. נכנסתם לאתר, בחרתם סרט כמו בספרייה, והם שלחו בדואר. זה אפשר להם להחזיק הרבה יותר כותרים במלאי מאשר חנות פיזית. חנות פיזית צריכה עשרה עותקים מהסרטים החמים, אבל כמה סרטים אחרים אפשר להחזיק על מדף בכל חנות? אלף? אלפיים? אם יש לכם מחסן מרכזי אחד, אפשר להחזיק מאה אלף כותרים. אם מישהו רוצה סרט נדיר, שולחים לו. כך Netflix כבר הייתה בעמדה טובה יותר לשרת אנשים שרצו סרטים נדירים או פחות פופולריים. הקהל שלה היה ממוקד יותר.

הביצועים הראשוניים של חדשנות לרוב לא מתאימים לצרכים של השוק המרכזי. אבל החדשנות נכנסת, משתפרת ואז גדלה. דוגמה: אם מפתחים מזון חדש לאנשים עם מגבלה מסוימת, למשל רגישות ללקטוז, הטעם בהתחלה אולי בינוני. אבל אנשים עם המגבלה רוצים משהו חדש ויקנו. אם זה מבחן מוצלח, יש לכם משאבים ושוק, ואז אתם יכולים לשפר את המוצר ובהדרגה להיכנס לשוק המרכזי. זה קורה הרבה: נכנסים דרך צורך niche, ואם הוא מספיק גדול כדי לאפשר בניית תשתית ושיפור, ממשיכים לשוק גדול יותר.

עכשיו branding first. הרעיון הוא להתחיל למכור, או לפחות ליצור brand, הרבה לפני שמתחילים לבנות את המוצר. למה? כי לקוחות משלמים קשה להשיג. כמה מכם משלמים חשבונות בבנק? כשאתם משלמים חשבונות, אתם חושבים פעמיים לפני שאתם מוציאים כסף. ברגע שמבקשים מאנשים להכניס יד לכיס, זה לא קל. הדבר הראשון שצריך להתמקד בו הוא prospects ו-customers: מי הלקוחות שלכם, איך משיגים את תשומת הלב שלהם, איך משווקים להם, ואיך הם קונים מכם.

בואו נתחיל בדרך הישנה. לא המצאנו branding ו-marketing. איך חברות עשו את זה בעידן הפרהיסטורי שלפני האינטרנט? ניקח דוגמה פשוטה ורחבה: Tambor. מה הם עשו? הם הלכו לחנויות חומרי בניין ואמרו: ניתן לכם שלט חינם, אפילו נשים עליו את השם שלכם, ואתם תתלו אותו על החנות. כך השם שלהם הופיע בכל מקום. אחר כך השם הפך לשם עצם: טמבוריה. אתם רואים חנות עם שני שלטים, Tambor ו-Nirlat. עכשיו Nirlat בעמדת נחיתות, כי השם של Tambor נמצא בכל מקום. זה הכוח של branding first: יוצרים מותג, אנשים מכירים אתכם, גם אם החנות מוכרת מיליון דברים אחרים.

במקום לבנות את החברה סביב רעיון המוצר, צריך לבנות אותה סביב branding ו-marketing. עכשיו אעבור על כמה דוגמאות, רבות מהן חברות שבניתי או שאני בונה עכשיו, כדי שנוכל לדבר מניסיון אישי. תראו מה קורה כאשר עושים marketing first.

מה זה brand first? אני משתמש במילים branding ו-marketing כמעט לסירוגין, אבל הן לא אותו דבר. ל-brand יש דרישות מוגבלות. אינכם רוצים שאנשים יכירו את כל פיצ'רי המוצר או את המחיר המדויק. brand הוא כמו טמבוריה: אה, זו חנות, אני יודע איפה היא, אני יודע שהיא קשורה לצבע, וזהו. זו חברה טובה כי אני רואה את השם שלה בכל מקום. Brand הוא שם שאתם רוצים שהלקוח יסמוך עליו. אתם רוצים תחושה חיובית. תחושה היא לא לוגיקה ולא עובדות. אנחנו לא מתחתנים בגלל לוגיקה ועובדות; אנחנו מתחתנים בגלל רגשות. אתם רוצים שהלקוחות יתחתנו איתכם, לא יקנו רק את ההיגיון שלכם.

דיברנו על Apple ועל אנשים שעומדים בתור מחצות כדי לקבל את הדגם הראשון של iPhone. לא צריך להיות ספציפיים לגבי מה המוצר עושה. דיברנו על Kardashians ושאלנו מה הן עושות. אנחנו לא יודעים, אבל אם הן מציעות עוד קו בגדים או משהו אחר, אנשים מסתכלים. בניית brand לוקחת זמן. צריך הרבה חשיפות. אנשים שוכחים חשיפה חד-פעמית. מחקרים מראים שצריך לפחות שש חשיפות לפני שמתחילים לשים לב. לכן פרסום חוזר שוב ושוב. כדי לבנות brand, צריך לחשוף אנשים למותג הרבה פעמים.

דיברנו על long tail. עוד כמה רעיונות לבניית brand. יש מתודולוגיות נוספות שפיתחנו. דוגמה שונה מאוד: אין לנו כלום, אין רעיון ברור, ואנחנו רוצים לחדור לשוק. נניח שוק רופאי שיניים. אתם רוצים למצב את עצמכם כמומחים בשוק. איך עושים את זה? לוקחים רשימה של חמש מאות רופאי שיניים ושולחים להם מייל עם שאלון של שלוש-ארבע שאלות: האם אתם משתמשים בטכנולוגיה החדשה הזו? אם לא, למה לא? אם כן, למה כן? רובם יתעלמו. עשרה או חמישה עשר יענו. עכשיו יוצרים מצגת ואומרים: עשינו מחקר שוק מעמיק וגילינו שהטכנולוגיה הזו עדיין לא מוכנה, או כל מסקנה אחרת. זה מבוסס על עובדות אמיתיות — חמישה עשר אנשים.

שבועיים אחר כך שולחים שאלון נוסף, והפעם מצרפים את תוצאות השאלון הקודם. עכשיו אתם לגיטימיים. אתם אומרים: זה מה שגילינו על הטכנולוגיה הקודמת, עכשיו אנחנו בודקים טכנולוגיה אחרת. הפעם תקבלו שלושים תשובות, כי הוכחתם רצינות. אחרי כמה איטרציות, בהדרגה, תהפכו למומחים. לא כי אתם אומרים שאתם מומחים, אלא כי השוק מתחיל לראות בכם מומחים. אנשים ירצו לקרוא את מה שאתם כותבים כי אתם עושים מחקר מעניין בקרב העמיתים שלהם ומביאים תוצאות מעניינות. וכשאתם מדברים על המוצר שלכם, אנשים מקשיבים, כי אתם המומחים.

זה תהליך גנרי שאפשר לעשות כמעט בכל תעשייה. צריך להפוך למומחה, או מה שקוראים היום thought leader. אפשר לעשות זאת די בקלות כי קל לשלוח שאלונים. חלק מהאנשים יענו, ותתחילו לקבל traction. זה מעניין כי זה אמיתי: אלה אנשים שמגיבים.

לפעמים זה אפילו יוצר הזדמנות הכנסה. כבדיחה שאלתי כמה מגזיני דיג יש. יש יותר מארבעים. למה זה מייצר הכנסות? כי הרבה אנשים רוצים להגיע לדייגים ולמכור להם חכות, ציוד ופתיונות. תמיד יש מישהו אחר שרוצה להגיע לאותם אנשים. אם אתם חודרים לשוק רופאי השיניים ויש לכם newsletter שנקרא על ידי מאה אלף רופאי שיניים, כי אתם thought leader בתחום ומדברים על טכנולוגיה חדשה כל שבועיים, אנשים שירצו לפרסם שם ישלמו לכם. לכן כשעושים branding first מתחילים ליצור assets. הם שווים כסף ומקלים מאוד על מכירת המקדחה החדשה שלכם.

רציתי להראות שלוש חברות שבנו את כל העסק שלהן מלכתחילה על אסטרטגיית long tail: Indeed, Zillow ו-Yelp. Indeed היא פלטפורמת גיוס. נוסדה בנובמבר 2004. הם עשו משהו דומה למה ש-ZoomInfo עשתה: סרקו את האינטרנט וחיפשו job postings, באתרי חברות, job boards וכדומה, אגרגו את הכול ופרסמו. כל משרה הייתה עמוד נפרד, והם אספו סביבה הרבה דאטה וסידרו אותו כך ש-Google יציג אותם ראשונים כשמישהו מחפש product manager בתעשייה מסוימת. היום יש להם 15,000 עובדים. לקח עשרים שנה להגיע לשם.

Zillow הציגו מידע על כל כתובת. הדבר החשוב הוא engagement: הם רוצים שתבואו ותתבעו בעלות על ה-listing שלכם, ובשביל זה תשלמו קצת כסף. זו פלטפורמת נדל"ן, אבל הם עשו את זה חכם: לקחו כל כתובת בארצות הברית, והרבה מידע ציבורי מרשומות רבות, כך שזה לא היה קשה במיוחד.

הדוגמה שאני הכי אוהב היא Yelp. נוסדה ב-2004 והפכה לאחד המקורות המרכזיים לביקורות משתמשים, בעיקר סביב עסקים קטנים כמו מספרות, בתי קפה, עורכי דין וכדומה. הם התחילו מפרסום מידע של Yellow Pages. מישהו יכול לנחש מה זה Elio Technologies? כשייסדתי את ZoomInfo בשנת 2000, אי אפשר היה למצוא דומיין singlename.com. אז החלטתי להשתמש בשם עברי, Evyon, אבל גם זה היה תפוס, אז הוספתי i טיפשי. זה היה שם החברה ב-2004. גם החברה וגם הכתובת כבר לא קיימות, והחברה הפכה ל-ZoomInfo. שינינו את השם ב-2004. אבל Yelp עדיין מציג את הערך הישן של Elio, ממש מאתמול. זה מראה מאיפה הגיע הדאטה: מספר הטלפונים. הם מצאו אותו. לאף אחד אין קניין רוחני על עובדות. זו נקודה חשובה מאוד שאני רוצה שתחשבו עליה.
english_summary:
This lecture reviews earlier themes in digital innovation and develops the central idea of branding first. Innovation is described as evolutionary, enabled by existing technologies such as smartphones, GPS, the internet, databases, cloud computing, and search. Product innovation is different from scientific or technical innovation because it requires customers, persuasion, payment, and market timing. The lecture argues that being first is often dangerous: early entrants frequently misunderstand the market, while later entrants can learn from their mistakes and succeed once price, performance, and ease of use reach acceptable levels.

The lecture revisits sustaining and disruptive innovation. Sustaining innovation improves existing products for existing customers and usually supports higher profits, while disruptive innovation often begins with an inferior product or a new business model that incumbents overlook. Examples include subscription razors, Netflix, disk drives, Kodak, Blockbuster, pharma companies acquiring proven startups, and Google buying Android. The deeper point is that organizational DNA, existing customers, and scale needs make it difficult for large companies to respond to small or uncertain markets.

Most of the session explains branding first as a practical strategy for startups. A brand is not just a logo or product description; it is repeated exposure, trust, and positive emotion among the right customers. Google and SEO long-tail content are presented as a low-cost way to create awareness, engagement, and leads before the product is fully built. The Opster/Elasticsearch error-log strategy shows how obscure technical searches can become a beachhead, drive traffic, and feed a marketing funnel through a free checkup tool.

The lecture then applies the approach to GiveChop/Tikshat and IntelliChain. GiveChop builds a database of Israeli events, artists, venues, and cities to create long-tail pages, collect fan relationships, and offer paid tools to artists and municipalities. IntelliChain discovers that selling demand-planning software is too hard, so it sells S&OP training and strategic consulting first, using those interactions to learn the market and reshape the product strategy. The closing examples, including expert surveys, Indeed, Zillow, and Yelp, show that branding-first assets can create traffic, authority, revenue, and eventually easier product sales.
hebrew_summary:
ההרצאה מסכמת את הנושאים הקודמים בחדשנות דיגיטלית ומפתחת את הרעיון המרכזי של branding first. חדשנות מוצגת כתהליך אבולוציוני שמופעל על ידי טכנולוגיות ותנאים מאפשרים כמו סמארטפונים, GPS, אינטרנט, מסדי נתונים, ענן וחיפוש. חדשנות מוצרית שונה מחדשנות מדעית או טכנולוגית משום שהיא דורשת לקוחות, שכנוע, תשלום ותזמון שוק. המסר הוא שלהיות ראשון לעיתים מסוכן: השחקנים הראשונים לא תמיד מבינים את השוק, ואילו שחקנים מאוחרים יכולים ללמוד מהטעויות שלהם ולהצליח כאשר המחיר, הביצועים וקלות השימוש מגיעים לרמה מתאימה.

ההרצאה חוזרת להבחנה בין sustaining innovation לבין disruptive innovation. חדשנות משמרת משפרת מוצרים קיימים עבור לקוחות קיימים ותומכת ברווחיות גבוהה יותר, בעוד חדשנות משבשת מתחילה לעיתים במוצר נחות או במודל עסקי חדש שהחברות הגדולות מתעלמות ממנו. הדוגמאות כוללות סכיני גילוח במנוי, Netflix, דיסקים קשיחים, Kodak, Blockbuster, חברות פארמה שקונות סטארטאפים מוכחים, ו־Google שקנתה את Android. הנקודה העמוקה היא ש־DNA ארגוני, לקוחות קיימים וצורכי צמיחה מקשים על חברות גדולות להגיב לשווקים קטנים או לא ודאיים.

רוב ההרצאה עוסקת ב־branding first כאסטרטגיה מעשית לסטארטאפים. מותג אינו רק לוגו או תיאור מוצר; הוא חשיפה חוזרת, אמון ורגש חיובי אצל הלקוחות הנכונים. Google ו־SEO long tail מוצגים כדרך זולה ליצור awareness, engagement ולידים לפני שהמוצר בנוי במלואו. הדוגמה של Opster ו־Elasticsearch מראה כיצד חיפושים טכניים מאוד סביב error logs יכולים להפוך ל־beachhead, ליצור טראפיק ולהזין marketing funnel דרך כלי free checkup.

בהמשך ההרצאה מיישמת את הגישה על GiveChop/Tikshat ועל IntelliChain. GiveChop בונה database של אירועים, אמנים, אולמות וערים בישראל כדי ליצור עמודי long tail, לאסוף קשרים עם אוהדים ולהציע כלים בתשלום לאמנים ולעיריות. IntelliChain מגלה שקשה למכור תוכנת demand planning, ולכן מתחילה ממכירת קורסי S&OP וייעוץ אסטרטגי, ומשתמשת באינטראקציות הללו כדי ללמוד את השוק ולעצב מחדש את אסטרטגיית המוצר. הדוגמאות הסופיות, כולל סקרי מומחים, Indeed, Zillow ו־Yelp, מראות שנכסי branding first יכולים ליצור טראפיק, סמכות, הכנסות ובסוף מכירת מוצר קלה יותר.
